summary: KS1 (ages 5–7) first encounter with how breathing works: air enters through the nose/mouth, travels down the windpipe to the two lungs in the chest; the lungs take some oxygen (which the body needs to stay alive) from the air and add carbon dioxide (waste) to the breath we send back out. The core conceptual target is that the SAME air mixture goes in and out — changed, not swapped for pure gases — plus correct lung location (chest, not belly) and a felt reason we must keep breathing. Keep the diaphragm mechanism for later years; at KS1 'the chest gets bigger to pull air in' is the right grain. Activities centre on the child's own body and an animated, driveable breath model, with recognition checks kept as lighter scaffolds.
misconceptions: Thinking we breathe in pure oxygen and breathe out pure carbon dioxide, rather than the same air mixture with some oxygen removed and carbon dioxide added.
Believing air/breath goes into the stomach or belly rather than the lungs in the chest.
Thinking there is one lung, or not knowing lungs are in the chest.
Confusing breathing (air in/out) with eating/drinking, or thinking the windpipe and food pipe are the same tube.
Believing you breathe out ALL the oxygen, or that exhaled air has no oxygen left in it.
Thinking breathing is optional/voluntary only, not understanding the body needs a constant oxygen supply.

activities.title: Breathe with me: drive your own breath and watch the air change
steps: Put one hand on your ribs/chest and take a slow deep breath in, then let it out, feeling the chest rise and fall.
Using an animated model, tap-and-hold to breathe IN: watch the chest widen and a stream of air carrying oxygen dots flow in through the nose/mouth, down the windpipe, and puff up the two lungs.
Release to breathe OUT and watch the air leave: notice that some oxygen dots stayed behind in the body and new carbon-dioxide dots have joined the outgoing breath.
Say in your own words what changed about the air between going in and coming out.
Watch a 'hold your breath' meter climb until the body insists on a breath, and connect this to why air must keep coming.
activities.insight: Breathing is a repeating in/out process: the SAME air goes in and out but is changed — the lungs take some oxygen (which the body needs to live) and add carbon-dioxide waste. We can't stop breathing because the body keeps needing oxygen.

activities.title: See your warm breath on cold glass
steps: Take a deep breath and breathe out slowly with an open mouth ('haaa') onto a cold mirror or window.
Look at the fog that appears and feel that the breath is warm and moist.
Say what this shows: we really do breathe something out, and it is different from ordinary room air.
activities.insight: Exhaled air is real and carries moisture and warmth from inside the body — evidence that we breathe something out, not nothing, and that the out-breath differs from the in-breath.

activities.title: Trace the air path and find your lungs
steps: On a chest illustration, tap nose/mouth → windpipe → the two lungs to trace where air goes.

Put hands on your tummy and on your chest, take a big breath, and decide where the air actually goes inside you — then check that the air travels to the lungs in the chest, not into the belly or stomach.

Answer a lift-the-flap question: 'Do our lungs take ALL the oxygen out of the air?' → reveal 'No — they take just some, so the air we breathe out still has oxygen in it, and carbon dioxide has been added.'
Place the lungs correctly: a myth-buster flap shows two lungs in the chest, not one, and not in the belly.
activities.insight: Air travels nose/mouth → windpipe → two lungs in the chest; breathing is separate from the stomach/eating, and the out-breath still contains some oxygen.

activities.title: Quick checks: order the path and name the waste
steps: Put the air path in order: nose → windpipe → lungs.
Choose what we breathe out as waste (carbon dioxide).
Decide true or false: 'The lungs are in the chest.'
activities.insight: Recall the air path, the location of the lungs, and that carbon dioxide is the waste we breathe out.

activities.title: Talk it through with friendly lungs
steps: Respond to a friendly-lungs character that asks you to take a deep breath and breathe out slowly with an open mouth ('haaa') onto a cold mirror.
Explain to the character what you just saw and felt.
Answer the character's question: 'Why can't I stop breathing?'
activities.insight: Putting the experience into words — what was seen, felt, and why the body needs air — consolidates the idea that the body must keep getting oxygen.

checkQuestion: When you take a big breath in, where does the air actually go inside you, and why does your body want it? And is the air you breathe out exactly the same as the air you breathed in, or different — and how?
checkAnswer: The air goes down the windpipe into the lungs (not the tummy). The body wants it because the lungs take OXYGEN out of the air, and the body needs oxygen to stay alive. The air breathed out is different — it has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, which the body doesn't need — so breathing out gets rid of waste carbon dioxide.
